tool.name: Next.js
tool.tagline: Full-stack React framework with file-based routing, Server Components and caching
tool.description: Next.js is the most widely used React framework: it adds file-system routing, server rendering, React Server Components, Server Actions, caching and built-in optimisations for images, fonts and metadata. With the App Router you build full-stack apps where data fetching and mutations live next to the components that use them. It deploys to Vercel, any Node.js server, containers or static hosting.

glossary.def: Next.js's way of building an app from the app folder: each folder inside it is one part of a URL, and special files such as page.tsx say what to show there.
Next.js's older way of building apps, from a pages folder. It still works, but new projects use the App Router.
One part of a URL between slashes, such as blog in /blog/hello. In the App Router each one matches a folder inside app.
The layout in app/layout.tsx that wraps every page of a Next.js app. It is required and holds the page's <html> and <body> tags.
The bundler built into Next.js (the default since version 16): it turns your files into code the browser can load, fast enough to update the page as you save.
Next.js 16's caching model, switched on in new apps: pages are built ahead of time as far as possible, and you choose what to keep and reuse with 'use cache'.
A program that runs JavaScript outside the browser, on your computer or a server. Next.js, npm and most JavaScript tools need it installed.
A string such as 'use client' written alone at the very top of a file or function, telling React or Next.js how to treat that code.
A route folder whose name is in square brackets, like [slug], so one page serves many URLs; the matching part of the URL is handed to the page as a value.
Moving to another page inside the app without the browser reloading: Next.js fetches only what changed and swaps it in, so shared parts of the screen stay as they were.
Loading what the next page needs in the background before the user clicks, so it can appear at once when they do.
A route.ts file in a Next.js app folder that answers HTTP requests with your own code and returns data such as JSON instead of a page.
A styling tool where you style elements with many small ready-made class names, like p-4 for padding, written straight in your JSX.
CSS files named like card.module.css whose class names are renamed to unique ones, so their rules apply only where the file is imported.
Content jumping around while a page loads, for example text pushed down when an image appears late above it.
A speed measure: how long until the biggest image or block of text in the first screen of a page has appeared. Search engines use it to rate pages.
To build a page's HTML ahead of time, usually when the app is built, so a ready copy can be sent instantly instead of being made for each visitor.
Next.js sending the parts of a page that were built ahead of time instantly, and filling in the parts that need the visitor's request as they become ready.
A label you attach to cached results with cacheTag, so that later one call can throw away every result carrying that label.
In Next.js, to mark cached data or pages as out of date so they are made again with fresh data, either after a set time or right after a change.
A caching approach: when a cached copy is out of date, hand it out once more right away while a fresh copy is made in the background.
A guarantee that after you change something, you see your change straight away, rather than an older cached copy.
A content management system: a website or app where editors write and publish articles and pages without touching code.
Showing two versions of a page to different visitors and measuring which works better, such as which button gets more clicks.
A Next.js folder whose name is in parentheses, like (marketing): it groups pages and can give them their own layout without becoming part of the URL.
A Next.js folder starting with @, like @team, whose page is handed to the layout as an extra prop, so one layout can show several pages side by side.
A Next.js folder named with (.) or (..) that shows another route inside the current page, such as in a pop-up, when you navigate to it within the app.
One place in your server code, a set of functions, that every read of protected data goes through, and that checks who is asking before returning anything.
A data transfer object: a small object holding only the fields another part of the system needs, instead of the whole stored record.
Incremental Static Regeneration: in older Next.js apps, a page built ahead of time that is rebuilt in the background at most every so many seconds.
Settings a Next.js page or layout file exports as named values, such as export const revalidate = 60, used by the older caching model.
Where the Next.js router keeps page data it has fetched or prefetched in the browser, so revisiting or going back can be instant.
The hard-to-guess ID Next.js gives each Server Function at build time. The browser sends it with a request to say which function to run.
A build step that leaves out code nothing uses, so it isn't shipped or reachable.
When a browser still running an old version of an app talks to a server already running the new one, and they no longer match.
Building a Next.js app into plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript files that any simple file host can serve, giving up the features that need a server.
An older, lighter place for Next.js code to run, with fewer features than Node.js. It is deprecated in favour of Node.js.
The piece that decides where Next.js stores cached results, for example a shared store that several copies of the app can all use.
The company that makes Next.js, which also runs a hosting service for publishing web apps.
Search engine optimisation: making pages easy for search engines to find, understand and show well in their results.
A standard set of page tags (title, description, image) that apps and social networks read to build the preview card when someone shares a link.
A file listing a website's pages, usually /sitemap.xml, so search engines can find all of them.
The visible area of a web page in the browser window or phone screen.

concepts.name: Creating a Next.js app
concepts.summary: Create a project with create-next-app, run it on your computer, and find your way around the files and folders it makes.
concepts.why: Knowing where things live in a new project makes every later Next.js idea easier to place.
concepts.body:
In the React lessons you set up projects with Vite, and everything ran in the browser. **Next.js** is a framework built on React that also runs part of your app on a server, and adds ready-made answers for pages, URLs, loading data and publishing. You start a project with one command in the terminal:

```bash
npx create-next-app@latest my-app
cd my-app
npm run dev
```

`npx` runs a package's command without installing it first; accept the recommended answers to its questions. `npm run dev` starts the dev server at `http://localhost:3000`. It runs on **Node.js**, the program that runs JavaScript outside the browser, so you need it installed.

The defaults add TypeScript, Tailwind CSS for styling, ESLint (a linter) and **Cache Components**, Next.js 16's caching model, covered later. The code in these lessons is TypeScript: labels like `: string` or `{ children: React.ReactNode }` only describe what a value is, so you can read past them.

Three commands in `package.json` matter:

- `next dev` — the dev server, with Fast Refresh. It uses **Turbopack**, the bundler built into Next.js.
- `next build` — prepares the finished app for publishing and lists every page it found.
- `next start` — runs that finished app as a real server.

The key folders and files:

- `app/` — your pages. Each folder inside becomes part of a URL, and special files such as `page.tsx` say what to show. This way of building is called the **App Router**.
- `app/layout.tsx` — the **root layout**: a component that wraps every page and holds the `<html>` and `<body>` tags. It is required.
- `public/` — files sent to the browser exactly as they are: `public/logo.svg` appears at `/logo.svg`.
- `next.config.ts` — settings for Next.js itself.
- `.env` files — settings such as passwords that stay out of your code (a later lesson).

In imports, `@/` means the project's top folder, so `@/lib/db` works from any file.

Tutorials for the older **Pages Router** use a `pages/` folder instead. It still works, but new projects use the App Router, and so do these lessons.

One big change from Vite: components in `app/` run on the server by default, not in the browser. The lesson on Server and Client Components explains what that means and why it helps.
takeaways: `npx create-next-app@latest` sets up a project; `npm run dev` runs it on your computer
Pages live in `app/`; `app/layout.tsx` is the required root layout with `<html>` and `<body>`
`next dev`, `next build` and `next start`: work on the app, prepare it for publishing, run the finished app
pitfalls: Following a Pages Router tutorial (a `pages/` folder, `getServerSideProps`) in an App Router project; the two work differently.

quiz.q: Which file must exist at the top of the app directory and render <html> and <body>?
quiz.explain: The App Router requires a root layout, app/layout.tsx, which renders the html and body tags around every page.

concepts.name: Pages, layouts and file-based routing
concepts.summary: Create pages with folders and page files, and share parts of the screen between pages with nested layouts.
concepts.why: File-based routing is the backbone of every Next.js app; layouts save you repeating the same header and menu on every page.
concepts.body:
In a Vite app you chose screens with a router library. In the App Router the **folders are the routes**: each folder inside `app/` is one **route segment**, one part of the URL between slashes. Special files inside the folder say what to show there.

- `page.tsx` exports the page's component and makes that URL exist. `app/page.tsx` is `/`, `app/blog/page.tsx` is `/blog`, `app/blog/archive/page.tsx` is `/blog/archive`.
- `layout.tsx` wraps every page below it. It receives the page (or a deeper layout) as `children` and draws the shared parts around it, such as a menu.

A folder without `page.tsx` isn't a URL, so you can keep components, tests and styles right next to the pages that use them. Starting a folder name with an underscore (`_components`) makes that intent clear.

**Layouts nest**: `app/layout.tsx` wraps `app/dashboard/layout.tsx`, which wraps `app/dashboard/settings/page.tsx`. When the user moves between pages under the same layout, the layout is not re-rendered and keeps its state: an open sidebar or text typed in a search box stays as it was. Only the part that changed is drawn again.

If you want a wrapper that starts fresh on every page change instead, name the file `template.tsx`. Pages and layouts may also be `async` functions, because by default they run on the server (the next lessons explain).

Other special files you will meet soon: `loading.tsx` (what to show while a page loads), `error.tsx` (what to show if something breaks), `not-found.tsx` (the "page doesn't exist" screen) and `route.ts` (a URL that returns data instead of a page).
takeaways: Folders are URL segments; `page.tsx` makes a segment a real URL
`layout.tsx` wraps the pages below it and keeps its state as the user moves between them
Folders without `page.tsx` (or starting with `_`) can safely hold other files
pitfalls: Keeping per-page data or state in a layout and expecting it to reset when the user moves to another page; layouts stay as they are.

quiz.q: You navigate from /dashboard to /dashboard/settings. What happens to the dashboard layout?
options: It stays mounted and keeps its state; only the page part changes
The whole page reloads in the browser
It runs again but loses its state
quiz.explain: Layouts are kept while moving between the pages inside them, so their state survives.

concepts.name: Linking and navigation
concepts.summary: Move between pages with <Link>, see how Next.js loads the next page early, and navigate from your own code with useRouter.
concepts.why: Fast page changes are a key Next.js benefit, and they depend on using Link and the navigation Hooks correctly.
concepts.body:
A plain `<a href="/blog">` makes the browser throw the current page away and load a new one from scratch. Next.js's **`<Link>`** component, from `next/link`, avoids that. `<Link href="/blog">Blog</Link>` still renders an `<a>`, but clicking it does a **client-side navigation**: Next.js fetches only the parts of the page that changed and swaps them in. Layouts keep their state and the browser doesn't reload.

Links also **prefetch**. In the finished app, when a link scrolls into view or the mouse hovers over it, Next.js quietly loads what that page needs, so it is often ready before the click. By default it loads the parts of the page that are the same for every visitor. For a rarely used link, turn this off with `prefetch={false}`.

To navigate from your own code, use the Hooks from `next/navigation`. Like all Hooks they only work in components that run in the browser, which need `'use client'` at the top of the file (the next lesson explains):

- `useRouter()` — `router.push('/path')` goes to a page, `router.back()` goes back, `router.refresh()` reloads the current page's data from the server.
- `usePathname()` — the current path, for example to highlight the active link.
- `useSearchParams()` — reads the query string (`?q=next`).
- `useParams()` — the values of the changing parts of the URL (a later lesson).

In code that runs on the server, call `redirect('/login')` from `next/navigation` to send the user to another URL instead. It works by throwing a special error that Next.js catches, so code after it never runs.

Use plain `<a>` tags for links to other websites.
takeaways: `<Link>` swaps in only what changed, without a full reload, and prefetches in the finished app
`useRouter`, `usePathname` and `useSearchParams` come from `next/navigation` and need a `'use client'` file
On the server, `redirect()` sends the user elsewhere; it throws, so code after it doesn't run
pitfalls: Importing `useRouter` from `next/router` (the older Pages Router) in an App Router component; use `next/navigation`.

quiz.q: Why prefer <Link href="/blog"> over <a href="/blog"> for internal links?
options: a tags don't work in Next.js
Link keeps the page in memory forever
Link is required for search engines to find the page
Link swaps in only what changed and prefetches, instead of reloading the whole page
quiz.explain: Link does a client-side navigation and prefetches; a plain a tag makes the browser reload the whole page.

concepts.name: Dynamic routes, params and searchParams
concepts.summary: Make one page serve many URLs with [slug] folders, and read the URL's values from params and searchParams.
concepts.why: Blog posts, products and user profiles are all dynamic routes, and the way you read their values changed in recent versions.
concepts.body:
A blog can't have one folder per post. Instead, wrap a folder name in square brackets to make a **dynamic segment**: `app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx` matches `/blog/hello-world`, `/blog/my-trip` and so on. Whatever is in that position of the URL is handed to the page under the name `slug`.

- `[...slug]` is a **catch-all**: it matches several parts at once, so `/docs/a/b/c` gives `slug = ['a', 'b', 'c']`.
- `[[...slug]]` is an **optional catch-all** that also matches `/docs` with nothing after it.

Pages receive two props: **`params`**, the values of the dynamic segments, and **`searchParams`**, the values from the query string (`?color=red`). Both are Promises (since Next.js 15), so the page is an `async` function that `await`s them:

```tsx
export default async function Page({ params }: PageProps<'/blog/[slug]'>) {
  const { slug } = await params
}
```

`PageProps<'/blog/[slug]'>` is a TypeScript label that Next.js writes for you from your folders (when you run `next dev` or `next build`). It tells your editor exactly which params this page has; the code would run the same without it. Layouts get `LayoutProps` the same way, with `params` but no `searchParams`.

In components marked `'use client'`, use the `useParams()` and `useSearchParams()` Hooks instead, or React's `use(params)`, which waits for a Promise inside a component.

Params are always strings (or arrays of strings for catch-alls), so convert and check them yourself. Call `notFound()` when, say, no post has that slug: Next.js then shows its "not found" page.

Normally a dynamic page is built when someone asks for it, because its values aren't known in advance. Listing values with **`generateStaticParams`** lets Next.js build those pages ahead of time; a later lesson covers it.
takeaways: `[slug]`, `[...slug]` and `[[...slug]]` folders make dynamic segments
`params` and `searchParams` are Promises: `await` them (or use the Hooks in `'use client'` files)
`PageProps<'/route'>` gives them the right types automatically
pitfalls: Reading `params.slug` without awaiting `params` first; since Next.js 15 it is a Promise.

quiz.q: For the file app/docs/[...slug]/page.tsx, what is the awaited params.slug for /docs/guides/intro?
quiz.explain: A catch-all segment gives an array of the URL parts it matched.

concepts.name: Server and Client Components
concepts.summary: Learn which components run on the server and which in the browser, how 'use client' switches, and what you can pass between them.
concepts.why: Every design decision in an App Router app follows from where each component runs.
concepts.body:
In a Vite app, all your components run in the visitor's browser. The browser is the **client**: the program that asks a server for pages and shows them. In the App Router it's the other way round: components run on the server unless you say otherwise. These are called **Server Components**.

Because a Server Component runs on your server, it can do things browser code never should. It can be `async` and read straight from a **database**, the program that stores your app's data. It can use **secrets**, such as passwords, that must never reach visitors. And its own code is never sent to the browser, so it adds nothing to the download.

The catch: a Server Component runs once to produce its output and is then done. It can't use state, Effects or event handlers like `onClick`, and it can't touch browser features.

For the interactive parts, write a **Client Component**: put `'use client'` at the top of the file. That line is a **directive**, an instruction to React and Next.js. The file, and everything it imports, joins the JavaScript sent to the browser.

Client Components still get a head start on the server: Next.js renders them to HTML there first, so the page appears quickly. Building the HTML on the server like this is called **server-side rendering**.

In the browser, React then takes over that HTML, attaching state and event handlers so the page responds to clicks. That step is called **hydration**.

Rules for mixing the two:

- A Server Component can render a Client Component and pass it props, but only values that can be turned into text and sent over the network: strings, numbers, plain objects and arrays, dates, JSX and Promises. Ordinary functions and class instances can't cross.
- A Client Component can't import a Server Component, but it can receive one as `children`. That is how a client wrapper, such as a context provider or a pop-up, goes around server content.
- Put `'use client'` as low in the tree as you can: make the button interactive, not the whole page, so less JavaScript is downloaded.

For files that must never reach the browser, add `import 'server-only'` at the top: the build then fails if a Client Component imports them.
takeaways: Components in `app/` are Server Components by default: they can be async, read data directly and send no code to the browser
`'use client'` makes a Client Component for state and events; its props must be plain values that can be sent
Pass Server Components into Client Components as `children`; keep the `'use client'` parts small
pitfalls: Adding `'use client'` to a page or layout, which turns everything it imports into browser code.

quiz.q: A Server Component wants to give a Client Component an onClick handler defined in the server file. What happens?
options: It runs on the server when clicked
It fails: ordinary functions can't be sent from the server to the browser
Next.js copies the function into the browser automatically
quiz.explain: Only values that can be turned into text, such as strings, plain objects and JSX, can go from a Server Component to a Client Component; ordinary functions can't.

concepts.name: Fetching data in Server Components
concepts.summary: Load data by making a Server Component async and awaiting it, avoid slow chains of requests, and share repeated calls with cache().
concepts.why: Loading data on the server is the default and most efficient way to get data into an App Router page.
concepts.body:
In the React lessons you fetched data in an Effect, with loading flags and an `ignore` flag for replies that arrive out of order. In the App Router you usually need none of that. Make the Server Component `async` and `await` the data right where you need it, from `fetch` or from your database code:

```tsx
export default async function Page() {
  const posts = await db.post.findMany()   // db: your database code
  return <PostList posts={posts} />
}
```

The data is loaded on the server before the HTML is sent. So there is no loading flicker in the browser, no extra request from the browser, and any passwords used to reach the data stay on the server.

Many apps talk to the database through an **ORM**, a library that lets you read and save records as ordinary JavaScript objects, as in `db.post.findMany()` above. Next.js works with any of them.

Things to know:

- `fetch` results are **not cached**: every request for your page fetches fresh data. Keeping results for reuse is something you switch on with `'use cache'`, covered later.
- If several components `fetch` the same URL while one page is being built, Next.js sends that request only once. For your own database functions, wrap them in React's `cache()` to get the same sharing.
- Each `await` waits for the one before it, so independent requests awaited one after another form a waterfall. Start them together with `Promise.all`. A later lesson shows how to let slow parts of a page appear on their own.
- Handle failures: check `res.ok`, then show a message, call `notFound()`, or throw an error to show the error page.

Fetching in the browser still has a place: for data that changes while the page is open, or that depends on what the user does there. Use a library like SWR or TanStack Query for that.
takeaways: Make a Server Component async and await data directly; no Effect needed
`fetch` isn't cached by default; the same fetch in one page build is sent only once
Start independent requests together with `Promise.all`; `cache()` shares repeated database calls
pitfalls: Awaiting independent requests one after another, so the page takes the sum of their durations.

quiz.q: Two independent requests take 300 ms and 500 ms. They are awaited sequentially in a Server Component. Roughly how long until the page can render?
options: 0 ms, because the server is fast
quiz.explain: Awaits in a row add up; with Promise.all both run at once and it takes about 500 ms.

concepts.name: Styling: global CSS, CSS Modules and Tailwind
concepts.summary: Style a Next.js app with global CSS files, CSS Modules that apply to one component, and Tailwind CSS.
concepts.why: Every app needs styles, and Next.js supports several approaches with a few rules about where to import them.
concepts.body:
Next.js supports the styling approaches from the React lessons with no setup, plus a few rules about where to import them.

**Tailwind CSS** is set up in new projects. The only line it needs is `@import "tailwindcss";` in `app/globals.css` (the starter project also adds the small add-on that reads it). Then style with its small ready-made classes: `className="flex gap-4 p-6 text-lg"`.

**Global CSS**: import a CSS file in the root layout (`import './globals.css'`). Its rules apply to every page, so keep it for the basics: resets, fonts, colours and CSS variables. You *can* import a global CSS file from any component, but it still applies everywhere, so the root layout is the clearest place.

**CSS Modules**: a file named `*.module.css` only affects the components that import it. Import it as an object and use its class names: `import styles from './card.module.css'`, then `className={styles.card}`. Next.js renames each class to something unique, like `card_card__x7Yz`, so two components can both have a `.card` class without clashing. For Sass, a version of CSS with extras like nesting, install the `sass` package and use `.module.scss` files.

CSS-in-JS libraries that build styles in the browser while the app runs need extra setup and only work in `'use client'` components. Tailwind, CSS Modules and libraries that produce plain CSS files at build time work everywhere.

When you build the app, Next.js combines and shrinks the CSS and splits it per page, so each page downloads only the styles it uses. If two rules conflict, the one imported later wins, so import order matters.
takeaways: Tailwind is set up by default; it needs only `@import "tailwindcss"` in `globals.css`
Import global CSS in the root layout; it applies to every page
`*.module.css` files give a component its own uniquely renamed class names
pitfalls: Expecting a CSS Module class to apply when written as a plain string (`className="card"`); use `styles.card`.

quiz.q: What does importing styles from './button.module.css' give you?
options: Global CSS applied to every page
An object mapping your class names to unique names that only apply where the file is imported
quiz.explain: CSS Modules rename classes to unique names, so styles don't leak between components.

concepts.name: Optimised images and fonts
concepts.summary: Serve resized images that load only when needed with next/image, and fonts that don't make the page jump with next/font.
concepts.why: Images and fonts are the biggest causes of slow pages and content jumping around while loading; Next.js handles both with two components.
concepts.body: Big images make pages slow, and an image that pops in late pushes the text below it down. That jump is called **layout shift**, and it is easy to tap the wrong thing because of it. The **``** component from `next/image` replaces `` and fixes both: - It sends each device a copy resized for its screen, in a modern, smaller file format, and loads images only when they are about to scroll into view. - It needs the image's width and height so it can reserve the space. If you import the image file (`import hero from './hero.jpg'`), Next.js reads its size, and can show a blurred preview, automatically. For an image from another website, give `width` and `height` yourself, or `fill` to fill its parent box, with `sizes` saying how wide it will appear. Images from other websites are refused unless you list those sites in `next.config.ts` under `images.remotePatterns`. For the big image at the top of the page, the one visitors see first (speed tools call it the **Largest Contentful Paint** element), add `preload` so it starts downloading early. Older code uses `priority` instead of `preload`. Next.js 16 marks `priority` as **deprecated**: it still works for now, but it will be removed. **`next/font`** handles fonts. It downloads them once, when you build the app, and serves them from your own site, so visitors' browsers never contact Google Fonts. It also sizes the stand-in font to match, so text doesn't jump when the real font arrives: ```tsx import { Inter } from 'next/font/google' const inter = Inter({ subsets: ['latin'] }) ``` Add `variable: '--font-inter'` to use the font through a CSS variable (handy with Tailwind). `next/font/local` loads font files from your project. Create each font once in a shared file and import it where needed; every call creates a separate copy.
takeaways: `<Image>` resizes images and loads them only when needed; width and height prevent layout shift
Allow other sites' images with `images.remotePatterns`; add `preload` to the main image at the top
`next/font` downloads fonts at build time and serves them from your site without layout shift
pitfalls: Using an image from another website without width and height (or `fill`), or without a matching `remotePatterns` entry; Next.js refuses it.

quiz.q: When does next/font/google download the font files?
options: On every page request from the user's browser to Google
At build time; they are then served from your own domain
quiz.explain: next/font fetches and self-hosts fonts during the build, so no runtime requests go to Google.

concepts.name: Loading UI and streaming
concepts.summary: Show a loading state at once with loading.tsx and Suspense, and send slow parts of a page as soon as each one is ready.
concepts.why: Streaming keeps pages quick when some data is slow, and loading states make page changes feel instant.
concepts.body:
When a Server Component awaits slow data, nothing on the page can be sent until it arrives. **Streaming** fixes that: the server sends the HTML in pieces over the same response, the ready parts first and the slow parts as they finish, like a video that starts playing while it is still downloading. You mark where a page may be split with React's **``** component. `Loading...

}>` around a slow component shows the fallback straight away, then swaps in the real content when it is ready. Everything outside the Suspense boundary is sent immediately. Next.js gives you two ways to use it: - **`loading.tsx`** in a route folder wraps that folder's page in a Suspense boundary for you. Its component shows the moment the user navigates (the layout around it stays usable) and is replaced by the page when it's done. Because this loading state can be prefetched, even pages that need fresh data open instantly. - **``** around individual components gives finer control: each slow component streams in on its own when its data is ready. Make fallbacks look like the final content, such as grey boxes in the same layout (often called skeletons), so nothing jumps when the real content arrives. Give each independent slow part its own boundary, so they load in parallel instead of one slow part holding up everything. Streaming works with Client Components too. Start a fetch in a Server Component without `await`, pass the Promise to a Client Component, and read it there with React's `use(promise)` inside Suspense. Search engines' crawlers (the programs that read pages for search results) that can't handle streaming get the complete page instead; Next.js detects them. With Cache Components, Suspense boundaries also mark the parts of a page that must wait for a visitor's request, as the next lesson shows.
takeaways: `loading.tsx` wraps a route's page in Suspense automatically
`<Suspense>` around slow components streams each one in on its own
Separate boundaries let slow parts load in parallel without holding up the page
pitfalls: One Suspense boundary around the whole page, so the fastest content waits for the slowest.

quiz.q: A page has a heading and two slow components, each wrapped in its own Suspense boundary. What does the user see first?
options: A full-page spinner from loading.tsx always
The heading plus both fallbacks, then each component as its data arrives
quiz.explain: Content outside the boundaries is sent immediately and each boundary streams in independently.

concepts.name: Errors and not-found pages
concepts.summary: Treat expected errors as ordinary values, catch unexpected ones with error.tsx, and show missing things with notFound().
concepts.why: Good apps fail section by section instead of showing a blank page or a generic crash.
concepts.body:
Next.js separates two kinds of errors.

**Expected errors**, such as a form filled in wrongly or a record another service doesn't have, are part of normal operation. Treat them as ordinary values: check for them and render a message. Don't throw for these. The Server Actions lesson shows the same idea for forms.

**Unexpected errors**, such as bugs or a database that is down, are different: throw, and let an **error boundary** catch them. An error boundary is a component that catches errors from the components inside it and shows a fallback message instead of a blank screen.

- `error.tsx` in a route folder wraps that part of the page in an error boundary. It must be a Client Component (`'use client'`). It receives `error` (whatever was thrown) and `retry`, a function that loads that part again. An error goes to the nearest `error.tsx` above it, so the layouts around it keep working.
- `global-error.tsx` handles errors in the root layout itself and must render its own `<html>` and `<body>`.
- `catchError` from `next/error` makes reusable error boundaries for single components.

In production, the messages of errors thrown in Server Components are hidden from the browser so they can't leak details. `error.digest` is an ID you can look up in your server's **logs**, the notes a server writes about what it does.

Error boundaries only catch errors thrown while rendering. Errors in event handlers, like a failing click handler, need `try`/`catch` and state.

**Not found**: call `notFound()` from `next/navigation` when the thing asked for doesn't exist. It shows the nearest `not-found.tsx` and sends a 404 status. `app/not-found.tsx` also handles URLs that match no page.
takeaways: Treat expected errors as values; throw only for unexpected failures
`error.tsx` is a `'use client'` error boundary per route, given `error` and `retry`
`notFound()` shows the nearest `not-found.tsx` with a 404 status
pitfalls: Writing `error.tsx` without `'use client'`; error boundaries need React in the browser, so Next.js rejects it.

quiz.q: A widget in /dashboard/analytics throws during rendering and only app/dashboard/error.tsx exists. What does the user see?
options: The dashboard's error UI in place of the dashboard segment, with the root layout still working
quiz.explain: An error goes to the nearest error boundary, which replaces that part of the page while the layouts above it stay intact.

concepts.name: Server Actions and forms
concepts.summary: Change data from forms with Server Functions: 'use server', form actions, useActionState for pending and error state, then refresh or redirect.
concepts.why: Server Actions are the App Router's built-in way to handle forms and other changes without building your own server URLs for them.
concepts.body:
Reading data happens in Server Components. But when a user submits a form or clicks Delete, code in the browser has to ask the server to change something. A **Server Function** makes that easy: an `async` function marked with the `'use server'` directive. It runs on the server, yet browser code can call it like a normal function; Next.js sends the request behind the scenes. A Server Function used to change data is called a **Server Action**.

Define them in a file that starts with `'use server'` (every export becomes one), or inside the body of a function in a Server Component. Client Components can import them from such a file but can't define them.

Pass one to a form: `<form action={createTodo}>`. React calls it with the form's `FormData`, as in the React forms lesson; React calls a function used this way an **Action**. These forms work even before the page's JavaScript has loaded, an approach called **progressive enhancement**, and the page doesn't reload.

After changing data, update what the user sees:

- `refresh()` from `next/cache` reloads the current page's server data,
- `revalidatePath('/todos')` and related functions refresh cached data (covered with caching),
- `redirect('/todos/1')` goes to another page (it throws, so call it last).

For a pending flag and error messages, use React's **`useActionState(action, initialState)`** in a Client Component. It returns `[state, formAction, pending]`. Your action then receives `(prevState, formData)` and returns the new state, such as `{ error: 'Title is required' }`.

Security: each Server Action is a public **endpoint**, a URL that anyone can send a **POST** request to, not only your form.

So inside every action, check the input (**validation**, for example with the Zod library), check who is calling (**authentication**: are they logged in?) and whether they may do this (**authorization**).
takeaways: `'use server'` functions run on the server and can be passed to `<form action>`
`useActionState` gives state, a wrapped action and a pending flag
After a change: `refresh()`, revalidate, or `redirect()`
Every action is a public endpoint: validate input and check who's calling inside it
pitfalls: Relying on hiding a button as your authorization; anyone can send a POST request to the action directly.

quiz.q: Why must a Server Action check the user's permissions itself even if the button is only shown to admins?
options: Because actions run in the browser
Anyone can send a POST request straight to the action, so hiding the button protects nothing
quiz.explain: Actions are public endpoints that accept POST requests, so the permission check must happen on the server, inside the action.

concepts.name: Route Handlers (API endpoints)
concepts.summary: Build your own HTTP endpoints with route.ts files, using the same Request and Response objects as fetch.
concepts.why: Webhooks, mobile apps and file downloads need plain HTTP endpoints alongside your pages.
concepts.body:
Sometimes a URL should return data rather than a page: a mobile app asking for JSON, or another service telling you a payment went through. URLs like that make up an **API**, a set of operations other programs can call.

In Next.js you build one with a **Route Handler**: a `route.ts` file that exports functions named after HTTP methods, such as **`GET`**, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` and `DELETE`. It lives in `app/` like a page: `app/api/todos/route.ts` answers `/api/todos`. A folder can have `page.tsx` or `route.ts`, not both.

Handlers use the same `Request` and `Response` objects as `fetch`. They receive a `Request` (or `NextRequest`, which adds `nextUrl` and cookie helpers) and return a `Response`; `Response.json(data, { status: 201 })` is the usual shortcut.

- Read a JSON body with `await request.json()`, a form with `await request.formData()`, the query string with `request.nextUrl.searchParams`.
- Dynamic segments work as for pages: the second argument holds `params` as a Promise, typed with `RouteContext<'/api/todos/[id]'>`.
- `cookies()` and `headers()` from `next/headers` read the request's cookies and headers.

When to use them: for your own pages, read data in Server Components and change it with Server Actions. Use Route Handlers for things that must be real HTTP endpoints: **webhooks** (requests another service sends you when something happens, like Stripe after a payment), APIs used by mobile apps or other companies, the return step of a "Log in with Google" flow, generated files, and responses sent bit by bit.

Like Server Actions, Route Handlers are public: check who is calling and validate the input in every handler.
takeaways: `route.ts` exports GET, POST and other handlers that take a Request and return a Response
`params` arrive as a Promise in the second argument; type them with `RouteContext`
Use them for webhooks and outside apps; for your own pages prefer Server Components and Server Actions
pitfalls: Fetching your own Route Handler from a Server Component; call the data function directly and skip the extra trip over the network.

quiz.q: Your Server Component needs product data. A Route Handler at /api/products already returns it. What is the best approach?
options: Import and call the same data function the Route Handler uses, directly in the Server Component
Move the component to the client and fetch there
quiz.explain: Server Components can read data directly; an extra HTTP request to your own server only adds delay and code.

concepts.name: Metadata, SEO and OG images
concepts.summary: Set page titles, descriptions and link-preview data with the Metadata API, and generate preview images, sitemaps and robots files.
concepts.why: Metadata decides how your pages appear in search results and in link previews on social apps.
concepts.body:
Every page carries information that isn't shown on the page itself: its title in the browser tab, a description for search results, the picture shown when someone shares the link. This is the page's **metadata**, and it lives in the HTML `<head>`. Getting it right is a big part of **SEO** (search engine optimisation: helping search engines find and show your pages).

Next.js builds the `<head>` for you from a few special exports, together called the **Metadata API** (an API is the set of operations a library or service offers). You use them in layouts and pages that run on the server (not in `'use client'` files):

- **Fixed**: `export const metadata: Metadata = { title: 'About', description: '...' }`.
- **From data**: `export async function generateMetadata({ params })` returns metadata worked out from data, such as a blog post's title. If it fetches the same URL as the page, the request is sent only once.

Metadata **merges** from the root layout down: a page's `title` replaces its layout's, and anything it doesn't set is inherited. A layout can give a title format: `title: { template: '%s | Acme', default: 'Acme' }` turns a page's `title: 'Pricing'` into "Pricing | Acme".

The `openGraph` and `twitter` settings control link previews; **Open Graph** is the standard most apps read them from. `alternates.canonical`, `robots` and `icons` cover the rest. Set `metadataBase` in the root layout so short URLs like `/cover.png` become full ones.

**Special files** generate the rest:

- `opengraph-image.tsx` (or `.png`) is the preview picture. A `.tsx` one returns `new ImageResponse(...)` from `next/og`, which draws JSX into a PNG.
- `icon.png`, `apple-icon.png` and `favicon.ico` in `app/` become the site's icons.
- `sitemap.ts` and `robots.ts` return objects that become `/sitemap.xml`, a **sitemap** listing the pages you want search engines to find, and `/robots.txt`, rules for which pages their crawlers may visit.

Settings for the **viewport**, the visible area of the screen, such as the browser bar's colour, go in `export const viewport` or `generateViewport`.
takeaways: Export `metadata` or `generateMetadata` from server layouts and pages
Metadata merges from the top down; a title format in a layout adds the site name
`opengraph-image`, `icon`, `sitemap.ts` and `robots.ts` are special files
pitfalls: Writing `<title>` tags by hand or exporting metadata from a `'use client'` file; use the Metadata API in server files.

quiz.q: The root layout sets title: { template: '%s | Acme', default: 'Acme' } and a page sets title: 'Pricing'. What is the document title?
quiz.explain: The page's title is put into the layout's format in place of %s.

concepts.name: Environment variables and configuration
concepts.summary: Keep secrets and settings in .env files, expose only NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables to the browser, and configure Next.js in next.config.ts.
concepts.why: Leaking a secret into the browser's JavaScript is one of the most common and costly Next.js mistakes.
concepts.body:
Settings that differ between your laptop and the live site, such as the database address or a payment service's secret key, don't belong in your code. They go in **environment variables**: named settings handed to a program when it starts, like `DATABASE_URL=postgres://...`.

Next.js reads them from **env files**: `.env`, `.env.local`, `.env.development`, `.env.production` (and `.test` versions). If a name appears in several, the more specific file wins: `.env.local` beats `.env`. You can share `.env` with harmless defaults along with your code, but keep `.env.local`, with the real secrets, out of it.

The crucial rule: variables are **server-only by default**. `process.env.DATABASE_URL` works in Server Components, Server Actions and Route Handlers, but is `undefined` in the browser. Only names starting with **`NEXT_PUBLIC_`** reach browser code.

Those public values are pasted into the JavaScript files when you build the app. So changing one needs a new build, and anyone can read it in the browser. Never put a secret behind `NEXT_PUBLIC_`.

To stop server code from reaching the browser by accident, put `import 'server-only'` at the top of files that use secrets; importing them from a Client Component then fails the build.

**`next.config.ts`** holds settings for Next.js itself, as a typed `NextConfig` object. Common ones:

- `images.remotePatterns` — which other sites' images are allowed,
- `redirects()` and `rewrites()` — rules that send old URLs elsewhere, or show a different page at a URL,
- `headers()` — extra headers sent with responses, often for security,
- `output: 'standalone'` — a slimmed-down build for running in a **container**, a sealed package holding the app and everything it needs,
- `cacheComponents`, `reactCompiler`, `typedRoutes` and experimental switches.

Check that required variables are set when the app starts (the Zod library works well) so a missing one fails loudly instead of causing odd bugs later.
takeaways: Environment variables are server-only unless named `NEXT_PUBLIC_...`
`NEXT_PUBLIC_` values are baked in at build time and visible to everyone
`import 'server-only'` guards files that use secrets; `next.config.ts` holds framework settings
pitfalls: Renaming a secret key with a `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix so a Client Component can read it, which publishes it to every visitor.

quiz.q: A Client Component reads process.env.STRIPE_SECRET_KEY. What value does it get in the browser?
options: undefined, because only NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables are exposed to the client
An empty string after a warning
quiz.explain: Variables without the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix only exist on the server.

concepts.name: Prerendering and the static shell
concepts.summary: Learn what Next.js builds ahead of time, what must wait for a visitor's request, and how Suspense, connection() and generateStaticParams decide.
concepts.why: With Cache Components every page mixes parts built ahead of time and parts made per request; placing them well decides speed.
concepts.body:
Making a page fresh for every visitor takes time. If a page is the same for everyone, it is faster to **prerender** it: build its HTML once, when you run `next build`, and hand out that copy. Most pages are partly the same for everyone (header, product description) and partly personal (your cart).

With Cache Components (on in new apps), Next.js prerenders every page as far as it can. What completes becomes the **static shell**: the HTML plus the data React needs, ready to send instantly. Parts that need the actual request are left as holes and streamed in when someone visits. This mix is called **Partial Prerendering**.

Because the shell is the same for everyone, it can even be served from a **CDN**, a network of servers around the world that keep copies close to users.

What can be prerendered:

- fixed markup, imports and plain calculations,
- results of `'use cache'` functions and components (next lessons).

What can't, and so must sit inside a `<Suspense>` boundary so the rest of the page can still be prerendered:

- **request data**: `cookies()`, `headers()`, `searchParams`, and `params` not known at build time,
- **uncached data**: fetches and database reads without `'use cache'`,
- **values that must differ per request**, like `Date.now()` or `crypto.randomUUID()`; call `await connection()` first to say "wait for a real request".

If such code isn't inside Suspense, the development error overlay reports a **blocking route**: one where waiting for the request would hold up the whole page. It also suggests the fix. The deeper in the tree you wait for request data, the more of the page lands in the shell: pass the `params` Promise down to the component that needs it instead of awaiting it in a layout.

**`generateStaticParams`** lists dynamic segment values to prerender at build time, such as your 100 most popular product slugs. Other values get the shell instantly and their content on the first request.

Apps without Cache Components use an older model, where any request data makes the whole page wait for a request (a later lesson).
takeaways: Each page = a prerendered static shell + Suspense holes filled in per request
Request data, uncached data and per-request values must sit inside `<Suspense>`
`generateStaticParams` prerenders known params; `connection()` waits for a real request
pitfalls: Reading `cookies()` at the top of a layout, which pushes everything below it out of the static shell.

quiz.q: With Cache Components, a page reads cookies() in one small component. How do you keep the rest of the page prerendered?
options: Move cookies() into the root layout
You can't; any cookie read makes the page dynamic
Wrap that component in <Suspense> so only it renders at request time
quiz.explain: Suspense marks the cookie read as a hole; everything outside it stays in the prerendered static shell.

concepts.name: Caching with 'use cache'
concepts.summary: Cache functions, components and pages with the 'use cache' directive, set lifetimes with cacheLife and label entries with cacheTag.
concepts.why: Explicit caching is how Next.js 16 apps get prerendered speed for data that rarely changes, without surprise out-of-date data.
concepts.body:
Fetching the same product list for every visitor wastes time when it changes once a day. The **`'use cache'`** directive stores the result of an async function, component or whole page, and reuses it. Put it as the first line of the function body, or at the top of a file to cache everything the file exports.

- **Data**: `async function getProducts() { 'use cache'; ... }` shares the result wherever it's called.
- **UI**: a cached Server Component or page stores its rendered output.

Each stored result is filed under a **cache key**, its name in the cache. Next.js builds the key from the function itself, its **arguments**, and any outside variables it uses (it *captures* them, as closures do). So `getProduct('a')` and `getProduct('b')` get separate entries. Arguments and return values must be serialisable.

You can't call `cookies()` or `headers()` inside a cached function, since their values differ per visitor. Read them outside and pass the values in as arguments.

**`cacheLife(profile)`** sets how long a result stays fresh. Built-in profiles are `seconds`, `minutes`, `hours`, `days`, `weeks` and `max`, or give `{ stale, revalidate, expire }` yourself. Without it the `default` profile applies: the browser may reuse a result for 5 minutes, and the server makes a fresh one in the background once it is 15 minutes old. Very short lifetimes aren't put in the static shell; they're treated like request-time holes.

**`cacheTag('products')`** attaches a **cache tag**, a label, to an entry. When the data changes you can throw away every entry with that label at once; removing out-of-date entries like this is **cache invalidation**, the next lesson.

Where entries live: by default they're kept **in memory**, separately in each running copy of your app. `'use cache: remote'` stores them in a shared cache instead, and `'use cache: private'` caches personal data that reads cookies, only in that user's browser.
takeaways: `'use cache'` caches a function, component or page; arguments and captured values form the key
`cacheLife` sets how long entries stay fresh; `cacheTag` labels them for invalidation
Read cookies and headers outside and pass the values in; `use cache: remote` and `private` are variants
pitfalls: Calling `cookies()` inside a `'use cache'` function; request data isn't allowed in cached code.

quiz.q: getUser(id) uses 'use cache'. It is called with id 1 and then id 2. How many cache entries exist?
options: One, keyed by the function name
Two, because arguments are part of the cache key
One per page that calls it
quiz.explain: The cache key includes the arguments, so different ids give different entries.

concepts.name: Revalidating cached data
concepts.summary: Keep cached data fresh with lifetimes and on-demand refreshes: revalidateTag, updateTag, revalidatePath and refresh.
concepts.why: Caching is only safe if you can update it the moment the data changes.
concepts.body:
Cached data must become fresh again when the original changes. Making it fresh is called **revalidating**, and Next.js offers two ways.

**After a time**: the `cacheLife` profile says when an entry goes out of date. The next visitor still gets the old copy instantly while a new one is made in the background, an approach called **stale-while-revalidate**. After the `expire` time the old copy isn't served at all.

**On demand**, right after data changes:

- **`updateTag(tag)`** expires tagged entries at once, so the user who made the change sees it on the very next render (**read-your-own-writes**). It works only in Server Actions.
- **`revalidateTag(tag, profile)`** marks entries out of date, stale-while-revalidate style: one visitor may still get the old version while a fresh one is made. In Next.js 16 the second argument is required; `'max'` is recommended. It works in Server Actions and Route Handlers.
- **`revalidatePath('/blog')`** invalidates everything for one path (add `'layout'` to include the pages under it). Simple, but coarser than tags.
- **`refresh()`** re-renders the current page's uncached server data from a Server Action; it leaves tagged caches alone.

Choosing: when a user edits their own profile, call `updateTag` in the action. When an editor publishes in a **CMS** (a content management system, where editors write articles), the CMS sends a webhook to your Route Handler, which calls `revalidateTag('posts', 'max')`. Tag precisely (`post:42` as well as `posts`) so you refresh only what changed.

Every cache belongs to one **deployment**, one published version of your app: publishing a new version starts with freshly prerendered pages.
takeaways: `cacheLife` handles freshness over time
`updateTag` (Server Actions only) for read-your-own-writes; `revalidateTag(tag, 'max')` for background refresh
`revalidatePath` invalidates by URL; `refresh()` re-renders uncached data
pitfalls: Calling `revalidateTag('posts')` without the second argument, which Next.js 16 requires.

quiz.q: A user edits their profile in a Server Action and must see the change immediately. Which call fits best?
quiz.explain: updateTag expires the entries at once, so the user reads their own change; revalidateTag may serve the old version once.

concepts.name: Proxy (formerly Middleware)
concepts.summary: Run code before a request reaches your pages with proxy.ts: redirects, rewrites, headers and quick login checks, limited with a matcher.
concepts.why: Logic for every request, such as language redirects, A/B tests and quick login checks, belongs in Proxy.
concepts.body:
A **proxy** stands between a visitor and your app and can look at each request on the way through, like a receptionist. Next.js lets you run such code before a request reaches your pages: create `proxy.ts` in the project root (or `src/`) and export a function named `proxy` (or a default export). Only one such file is allowed, but it can import other modules.

Before Next.js 16 this feature was called **Middleware** (`middleware.ts`), the general name for code that sits between a request and the code that answers it. You'll still see that name in older projects.

The function receives a `NextRequest` and can:

- `NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/login', request.url))` — send the browser to another URL,
- `NextResponse.rewrite(url)` — show a different page while the address bar keeps the original URL,
- `NextResponse.next()` — let the request continue, optionally adding headers or cookies,
- return a `Response` directly.

Rewrites suit **A/B tests**, showing two versions of a page to different visitors to see which works better, and serving each customer's own site from one app by its domain.

Limit where it runs with `export const config = { matcher: [...] }`. Leave out images and other static files, or every file request pays the cost.

Proxy runs on Node.js in Next.js 16; the `runtime` setting that older code used to pick another environment isn't allowed in this file. It runs on every matching request, so keep it fast.

Good uses: redirects based on cookies or headers, sending visitors to their language, rewrites, security headers, and **optimistic login checks**: is there a session cookie at all? If not, redirect to the login page. Bad uses: slow data fetching, or being your only authorization check. Check access again next to the data, in each action and handler. For fixed redirects, use `redirects()` in `next.config.ts` instead.
takeaways: `proxy.ts` (formerly `middleware.ts`) runs before matching requests
Redirect, rewrite, set headers or respond; limit it with `config.matcher`
It runs on Node.js; keep it fast and use it only for quick, optimistic checks
pitfalls: Doing the only authorization check in Proxy; Server Actions and Route Handlers must check access themselves.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between NextResponse.rewrite and NextResponse.redirect?
options: rewrite serves another route while the browser URL stays the same; redirect tells the browser to go to a new URL
redirect works only for external URLs
rewrite changes the URL but not the content
quiz.explain: A rewrite happens inside the server; a redirect sends a 3xx response, and the URL in the browser changes.

concepts.name: Route groups, parallel and intercepting routes
concepts.summary: Organise routes with (groups), show several pages at once with @slots, and build pop-ups with their own URL using intercepting routes.
concepts.why: Dashboards, pop-ups with a shareable URL and sections with different layouts need routing beyond plain folders.
concepts.body:
**Route groups**: a folder name in parentheses, like `(marketing)`, groups routes without appearing in the URL. `app/(marketing)/about/page.tsx` is `/about`. Groups let different sections have different layouts, and even separate root layouts (each group with its own `layout.tsx` containing `<html>`).

**Private folders**: folders starting with an underscore, like `_lib` or `_components`, are left out of routing entirely.

**Parallel routes** show several pages side by side in one layout. Each is a named **slot**, a folder starting with `@`: `app/dashboard/@team/page.tsx` and `@analytics/page.tsx` reach `app/dashboard/layout.tsx` as `team` and `analytics` props, next to `children`. Each slot has its own loading and error states and can be shown conditionally, for example by the user's role.

Add `default.tsx` to a slot as what to show when the slot has nothing for the current URL after a full page load; without it you get a 404.

**Intercepting routes** show a route inside the current layout during a client-side navigation, while visiting the URL directly shows the full page. The folder names work like **relative paths**: `(.)photo` intercepts a sibling folder, `(..)` one level up, `(...)` from the `app` root.

Combined with an `@modal` slot, this gives a **pop-up with its own URL**: clicking a photo opens it in a dialog with a shareable address; refreshing shows the full photo page; Back closes the dialog.

**`template.tsx`** is like a layout but is mounted afresh on every navigation, for entry animations or per-page effects.
takeaways: `(group)` folders organise routes and layouts without changing URLs
`@slot` folders are parallel routes passed to the layout as props; add `default.tsx`
`(.)`, `(..)` and `(...)` intercept routes for pop-ups with their own URL
pitfalls: Forgetting `default.tsx` in a parallel slot, so a hard refresh of another URL renders a 404.

quiz.q: With @modal/(.)photos/[id] and photos/[id], what does a user see when opening /photos/7 directly in a new tab?
options: The modal over the previous page
The full photos/[id] page, because interception only applies to client-side navigation
quiz.explain: Interception only happens during client-side navigation; opening the URL directly shows the real route.

concepts.name: Authentication and data security
concepts.summary: Secure a Next.js app: sessions in cookies, a server-only Data Access Layer, checks in every action and handler, and only safe data for the browser.
concepts.why: The App Router blurs the line between server and browser code, so security mistakes easily leak data or let anyone change it.
concepts.body:
Signing in usually works through a **session**: after the user proves who they are, the server remembers them across requests, linked by a cookie. You can use a library (Auth.js, Clerk, Better Auth and others) or set your own session cookie in a Server Action at login and read it with `cookies()`.

That cookie must be safe in the browser's hands. Its contents are **encrypted** (scrambled with a secret key) or signed, so they can't be read or forged. It is also set `httpOnly` (page scripts can't read it), `secure` (only sent over HTTPS) and `sameSite` (not sent along from other sites' pages).

Where to check access:

- **Data Access Layer (DAL)**: one `server-only` module that checks the session and offers functions like `getCurrentUser()` and `getInvoices()`. Wrap the session check in React's `cache()` so it runs once per request. Every read of protected data goes through it.
- **Server Actions and Route Handlers**: check authentication and authorization inside each one; they are public endpoints.
- **Proxy**: only optimistic redirects (no cookie: go to login), never the only check.
- **Not layouts**: they may not re-render when the user moves between pages, so a check there can be skipped. Check in pages or the DAL, close to the data.

Limit what reaches the browser:

- Return a **DTO** (data transfer object): a small object with just the fields the screen needs, not a whole database record with, say, the password **hash**, the scrambled fingerprint stored instead of the password.
- Remember that every prop passed to a Client Component is sent to the browser.
- React's experimental *taint* functions (switched on with the `taint` config option) can mark an object or value as never allowed to reach the browser.

Finally, validate all input against a **schema** (a description of the expected shape, for example with Zod), **rate-limit** sensitive actions such as signing in (cap how often one user may try), and treat `searchParams` and `params` as **untrusted input**: anyone can type anything into a URL.
takeaways: Keep session checks in one `server-only` Data Access Layer, cached per request
Check permissions inside every Server Action and Route Handler; Proxy is only a quick first check
Return small DTOs; everything passed to Client Components is public
pitfalls: Checking auth only in a layout, assuming it protects all child pages and their data.

quiz.q: Why is checking authentication only in a shared layout insufficient?
options: Layouts may not re-render on navigation and don't protect the data functions, actions or route handlers
Layouts run only on the client
quiz.explain: Security checks belong close to the data: in the Data Access Layer, pages, actions and handlers.

concepts.name: Caching without Cache Components
concepts.summary: Read and maintain apps on the older caching model: fetch cache options, route segment config, unstable_cache and static vs dynamic routes.
concepts.why: Most existing Next.js 13 to 15 apps use this model, and you will maintain or migrate them.
concepts.body:
Apps that don't switch on `cacheComponents` use the **previous model**, which you will meet in most existing codebases (Next.js 13 to 15).

**A whole route is either static or dynamic.** At build time Next.js tries to prerender each route. Reading request data (`cookies()`, `headers()`, `searchParams`, `connection()`) or a `fetch` marked `cache: 'no-store'` makes the entire route **dynamic**: rendered again for every request. Otherwise it is **static**, built once, even if it fetched data during the build.

**Caching is set per request or per route:**

- `fetch(url, { cache: 'force-cache' })` caches one request; since Next.js 15 the default is not cached.
- `fetch(url, { next: { revalidate: 3600, tags: ['posts'] } })` caches it with a lifetime in seconds and tags.
- `unstable_cache(fn, keyParts, { revalidate, tags })` caches other work, such as database queries.
- **Route segment config**: named exports in a page or layout, such as `export const revalidate = 60`, `export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'` or `'force-static'`, `dynamicParams` and `fetchCache`.

`export const revalidate = 60` gives **ISR** (Incremental Static Regeneration): the page is static, but rebuilt in the background at most once every 60 seconds when visited.

On-demand updates use the same `revalidatePath` and `revalidateTag(tag, profile)` functions.

These route segment options are **removed** when Cache Components is on. Migrating means replacing `revalidate` exports and fetch options with `'use cache'` + `cacheLife`, and wrapping request-data reads in Suspense. The official migration guide walks through it.
takeaways: Previous model: a whole route is either static or dynamic
Cache with fetch options, `unstable_cache` and route segment config like `revalidate`
These options are removed under Cache Components; migrate to `'use cache'` + `cacheLife`
pitfalls: Copying `export const revalidate` into an app with Cache Components enabled, where it is no longer allowed.

quiz.q: In the previous model, a page reads cookies() in one small component. What happens to the route?
options: cookies() returns empty at build time and the page stays static
Only that component renders per request
The whole route becomes dynamic and renders on every request
quiz.explain: Without Cache Components, reading request data makes the entire route dynamic.

concepts.name: RSC payload, prefetching and the client cache
concepts.summary: See what actually travels over the network: the RSC payload, how the router prefetches and caches pages, and what makes navigation fast or slow.
concepts.why: Diagnosing slow navigation, out-of-date screens and heavy server load requires knowing how the App Router works under the hood.
concepts.body:
Each page is rendered on the server into the **RSC payload**, React's compact description of what the Server Components produced. It holds their output, placeholders saying which Client Component goes where (with a link to its code file), and the props passed to each. (A *payload* is simply the data a message carries.)

On a first visit the server also turns the payload into HTML. The browser shows that HTML at once; React then reads the payload to match it up and hydrate the Client Components.

On **client-side navigations** no HTML is fetched. The router asks for the RSC payload of the changed segments only and merges it into the current tree, so shared layouts keep their state. A Server Action's response carries both the action's return value and, if it revalidated data, a fresh payload for the current page, all in one **round trip** (one request and its reply).

**Prefetching**: `<Link>` prefetches routes as they scroll into view or on hover. With Partial Prefetching (the default in new apps), the router prefetches each route's App Shell: its static shell plus the data that only depends on the visitor's session. `prefetch={true}` also renders cached content that depends on the URL, per link, at the cost of one server call each.

Prefetched payloads live in the **client cache**, the router's store in the browser, for their `stale` lifetime (from `cacheLife`, or the `staleTimes` setting).

What makes navigation slow:

- dynamic routes with no `loading.tsx` or Suspense boundary: nothing can show until the server answers,
- dynamic params not listed in `generateStaticParams`,
- large payloads: props passed to Client Components are serialised into every payload,
- slow networks.

`useLinkStatus()` shows a pending state on the clicked link while its page loads.
takeaways: Server Components render to an RSC payload; HTML is only made for the first load
Navigations fetch payloads for the changed segments and merge them into the page
Link prefetches App Shells into a client cache with a stale lifetime
Missing loading boundaries and large props make navigation slow
pitfalls: Passing large objects to Client Components, bloating every RSC payload and HTML response.

quiz.q: During a client-side navigation between two pages that share a layout, what does the browser request?
options: The RSC payload for the segments that changed
Nothing; everything is precomputed in the bundle
The full HTML of the new page
quiz.explain: Client-side navigations fetch RSC payloads for the changed segments; shared layouts are reused.

quiz.q: A dynamic route has no loading.tsx and no Suspense boundaries. Why can navigation to it feel unresponsive?
options: It triggers a full page reload
Link doesn't work with dynamic routes
Nothing can be shown until the server finishes rendering, so the click appears to do nothing
quiz.explain: Without a loading boundary there is no fallback to prefetch, so the screen waits for the whole server response.

concepts.name: How Server Actions work
concepts.summary: The mechanics behind Server Actions: action IDs, POST requests, encrypted captured values, one-at-a-time calls, limits and new-version mismatches.
concepts.why: Knowing what goes over the network prevents security holes, slow code and errors after you publish a new version.
concepts.body:
When you build the app, the **compiler** (the build step that transforms your code) replaces each Server Function in the browser code with a reference: an **action ID**. The ID is encrypted and changes with every build, so it can't be guessed.

Calling the function sends a POST request to the current page carrying the ID and the serialised arguments. The server looks the function up, runs it, and streams back the result (plus, if needed, a fresh RSC payload). Only POST can call actions.

Built-in protections:

- **CSRF** (cross-site request forgery: another site tricking a logged-in user's browser into sending a request): the request's `Origin` header must match your site's address. Behind a proxy that changes the address, list the allowed ones in `serverActions.allowedOrigins`.
- The request body is capped at 1 MB by default (`serverActions.bodySizeLimit`).
- **Dead code elimination**: the build drops actions no browser code uses, so they have no public endpoint.

**Captured values**: values an inline action captures from its page (like an `id`) are encrypted, sent to the browser with the form, and sent back on each call. Don't rely on that to hide secrets; pass only references such as ids, and re-read the data on the server. If several copies of your app run side by side, give them all the same `NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY`.

Behaviour to design around:

- The browser **sends actions one at a time**; `Promise.all` over several actions won't run them in parallel. Do parallel work inside one action, or use Route Handlers for requests that don't change data.
- Actions are for changing data, not for reading it.
- Every new deployment has new IDs. A tab still running the old version gets "Failed to find Server Action"; this mismatch is called **version skew**. Roll out new versions gradually and offer a refresh.
takeaways: Actions become encrypted IDs, called with a POST request to the current page
A CSRF origin check, a 1 MB body limit and dead code elimination are built in
Captured values are encrypted but must still be treated as untrusted
Browsers send actions one at a time; each deployment changes the IDs
pitfalls: Using `Promise.all` to run several Server Actions at once from the browser; they are sent one after another.

quiz.q: A client calls three Server Actions with Promise.all. How are they executed?
options: The client dispatches them one at a time, each waiting for the previous
quiz.explain: Next.js sends one browser's Server Actions one after another, so the re-rendered page stays consistent.

concepts.name: Deployment, runtimes and self-hosting
concepts.summary: Publish Next.js on Vercel, your own Node.js server, containers or static hosting, and understand runtimes, cache handlers, after() and version skew.
concepts.why: How your app behaves in production (caching, scaling, streaming) depends on how and where you deploy it.
concepts.body:
To **deploy** is to put a built version of your app where users can reach it. The main options:

- **Node.js server**: `next build` then `next start`. Every feature works.
- **Containers** (Docker): set `output: 'standalone'` and the build produces a minimal server (`.next/standalone/server.js`) with only the packages it needs; copy `public/` and `.next/static` next to it.
- **Static export**: `output: 'export'` writes plain HTML and JavaScript to `out/` for any simple file host, but server features are gone (actions, per-request rendering, image optimisation by default, Proxy).
- **Platforms**: **Vercel**, the company behind Next.js, supports everything; other hosting platforms plug in through deployment adapters.

On your own server, put a **reverse proxy** such as nginx in front: a server that receives every request first and passes it on to your app. It handles **TLS** (the encryption behind HTTPS), **compression** (shrinking responses so they travel faster) and slow connections, so your app doesn't have to.

**Runtime** means the environment your code runs in. Pages, Route Handlers and Proxy run on Node.js. The older **Edge runtime** (`export const runtime = 'edge'`), a lighter environment with fewer features, is deprecated, and with Cache Components the `runtime` export isn't supported at all; remove it when you meet it in older code.

**Caching across copies**: a busy site runs several copies of the app side by side. Prerendered HTML is stored on each copy's disk and `'use cache'` entries in its memory, so copies can disagree. Configure a shared **cache handler** (the `cacheHandlers` setting, used by `'use cache: remote'`), and give all copies the same deployment ID and `NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY`.

**`after(fn)`** from `next/server` runs work after the response has been sent, such as **logging** or analytics, without making the user wait.

**Version skew**: after a deployment, browsers still running the old version may ask the new one for files or actions that no longer exist. A consistent `deploymentId` lets Next.js notice and do a full reload.
concepts.code:
# Dockerfile (standalone output)
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build                     # next.config.ts has output: 'standalone'

FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production PORT=3000
COPY --from=build /app/.next/standalone ./
COPY --from=build /app/.next/static ./.next/static
COPY --from=build /app/public ./public
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

# app/api/checkout/route.ts - log after responding
# import { after } from 'next/server'
# export async function POST(req: Request) {
#   const order = await createOrder(await req.json())
#   after(() => analytics.track('order', { id: order.id }))   // runs after the response
#   return Response.json(order, { status: 201 })
# }
takeaways: `next start` on Node.js supports everything; `output: 'standalone'` suits containers
`output: 'export'` produces static files but drops server features
Several copies need a shared cache handler, the same deployment ID and the same action key
`after()` runs non-urgent work after the response
pitfalls: Running several copies of your own server with the default in-memory cache and per-build keys, so caches disagree and actions fail.

quiz.q: Which config makes next build produce a minimal server.js with only the required node_modules for Docker?
quiz.explain: Standalone output finds the packages the server really uses and writes a self-contained server for containers.
